cards.text: Proverbs is a book of wise sayings from Solomon, son of David, king of Israel (Proverbs 1:1), and here a father talks straight to his son. "My son, keep your father’s commandment, and do not forsake your mother’s teaching." I spent YEARS in a drawer full of instruction manuals NOBODY kept, friend, but this one's worth hanging on to.

cards.question: The father wants his son to hold this teaching close. How close?

answers.text: Bound on his heart and tied around his neck
Written on the doorframe of his house
Kept on a scroll beside his bed

cards.text: Then the father tells his son what that teaching will do for him.

cards.question: The father says the commandment and the teaching only help his son while he’s up and walking around.

cards.text: Guiding him, watching over him, talking to him when he wakes up: it’s a GPS that never once says "recalculating" in THAT tone. Then the father calls this commandment a lamp and this teaching a light.

cards.question: The father calls this commandment a lamp and this teaching a light. A lamp helps a man see where to ___.

cards.text: He even calls the reproofs of discipline the way to life. Correction is like the oven timer, friend: LOUD, annoying, and the ONLY reason my batch isn’t charcoal.
Now the father gets to the point: all that light is there to keep his son away from someone.

cards.question: Who is the father’s teaching meant to keep his son away from?

answers.text: The evil woman with a smooth tongue
The slacker who sleeps all day
The stranger who asks for a pledge

cards.text: She’s the adulteress, and her tongue is smooth. I bet her words make the worst idea in town sound like a GREAT one.

cards.question: The father’s warning only starts once a man acts, not with what he wants in his heart.
The father tells his son not to be pulled in by two things about the adulteress. Which two?

cards.text: Then he talks cost: the levy of the prostitute is poverty. And then he turns to the adulteress.

cards.question: What does the father warn his son the adulteress preys upon?

cards.text: Back to the father and his son. Now he asks a question anybody who’s ever stood next to a hot oven can answer.

cards.question: The father’s question means a man can hold fire close and walk away with his clothes unburned.

cards.text: Then a second question: can a man walk on hot coals without scorching his feet? I grabbed a hot cookie sheet with my mustache ONE time, friend, and I STILL flinch every time the timer dings.

cards.question: The father’s fire and hot coals are a picture. What is he really talking about?
The father says a few men who touch another man’s wife will get away with it.

cards.text: Then the father brings up a thief. People don’t despise the thief if he steals to satisfy his hunger.

cards.question: But what happens to that hungry thief if he gets caught?

answers.text: He gets off with a warning
He pays back just what he took

cards.text: He must give up all the wealth of his house. Then the father turns from the thief to the man who commits adultery.

cards.question: The father says the man who commits adultery lacks ___ and destroys ___.

cards.text: Wounds and dishonor will land on that man, and his reproach will never be wiped away. It’s like that burnt spot on a baking sheet that NO amount of scrubbing gets off.
And then there’s the woman’s husband.

cards.question: What does the father say enrages that husband?
The father says a big enough gift will calm that husband down in the day of vengeance.

findings.problem: The opening card says a father is talking to his son, and every later card follows that, calling the speaker "the father." Proverbs 6:20 doesn't say the father is speaking. The speaker says "keep your father's commandment," which puts the father in the third person, so the text leaves the speaker open. The cards should keep it open, for example "the teacher" or "the speaker in Proverbs," and not name him as the son's father.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The right answer, that a lamp helps a man see where to walk, isn't something Proverbs 6:23 says. 6:23 calls the commandment a lamp and the teaching a light, and calls the reproofs the way to life. Linking the lamp to walking is an outside idea, so the card tests what lamps do in general, not the passage. It also cites 6:23 for an answer that verse doesn't give. Ask about what the text actually gives, such as what the reproofs of discipline are called (the way to life).

rule.text: Every fact and every verse number comes from that text.

findings.problem: All five true or false cards (stop 1 cards 4 and 11, stop 2 cards 2, 5 and 13) have False as the right answer. Most are worded with "only" or as a claim the passage plainly rules out. A baker could learn to tap False without reading the question.
findings.question: Should the docs require true or false cards to have a mix of True and False right answers across the walkthrough, or across each stop? The "No formula" rule covers which question type comes next, the order of types and where a blank falls. It doesn't say anything about which answer is right on true or false cards.
